title: I built a public paper-trading League for crypto bots: What would make you trust the results?
author: GreatBreadfruit8139
selftext:
One thing that has always bothered me about trading-bot results is how little context you usually get.

Someone posts a great backtest or a PnL screenshot, but you often don’t know whether the settings were changed halfway through, whether losing versions disappeared, how long the bot actually ran, or whether the “amazing APY” came from 6 trades in 4 days...

So I built a public Paper-trading League for crypto bots because I wanted a place where strategies could be compared in a more useful way than just looking at isolated backtests or screenshots.

The idea is simple: Traders, bot builders and strategy creators can put different approaches side by side, let them run over time, clone each other’s setups, create modified versions, and see how those variants actually behave under the same market conditions.

So instead of asking:

“Is this strategy good?”

you can start asking more useful questions like:

\* What happens if I change only the exit logic?  
\* Does this clone outperform the original?  
\* Does a simpler version hold up better?  
\* Which strategy has lower drawdown over the same period?  
\* Is the bot actually outperforming BTC or ETH?  
\* Does a strategy still look good after 30, 50 or 100 trades?  
\* What changed between V1 and V2?  
\* Which public variants are actually surviving over time?

That is the core idea behind the League: not just ranking bots, but creating a public environment where strategies can be tested, compared, copied, modified and improved over time.  

These aren’t just preset bots. You can configure the strategy directly in the League...     
The League currently supports long-only Spot strategies across USDT pairs, with configurable technical-entry/exit rules and DCA execution...

For entry and exit conditions, it currently supports:

\* RSI: configurable length, threshold and timeframe; above, below, crossing up or crossing down  
\* Stochastic: configurable %K length, smoothing, %D smoothing, threshold and K/D cross direction  
\* MACD: configurable fast/slow/signal lengths, signal-line cross and above/below-zero filtering  
\* Moving averages: SMA, EMA or WMA with configurable fast/slow lengths and bullish/bearish crosses  
\* ADX: configurable length and threshold  
\* Bollinger Bands %B: configurable period, standard deviation and threshold/cross  
\* Money Flow Index  
\* Commodity Channel Index  
\* Ultimate Oscillator: configurable short/middle/long periods  
\* Parabolic SAR: configurable step/max and price crossing above/below SAR  
\* Heikin Ashi: configurable number of consecutive bullish or bearish candles  
\* Price vs moving average / momentum: price above, below, crossing above or crossing below a configurable N-day average  
\* Average daily quote volume: configurable lookback and USDT-volume threshold as a liquidity filter

There are also a few internal strategy scanners currently available, including SMA Trend Long, TrendFrend / StrictRSI and Weekly Momentum.

Most conditions can be used as either Entry or Exit rules.

Multiple Entry conditions are combined with AND, and multiple Exit conditions are also combined with AND.

Conditions use closed candles, and the indicators can use different timeframes from 1 minute up to 1 month.

Then there’s the DCA/execution side.

You can configure:

\* one pair, selected pairs, or the supported USDT Spot universe  
\* Market or Limit base order  
\* base-order size  
\* safety-order size  
\* maximum safety orders  
\* how many safety orders remain active at once  
\* initial price deviation  
\* safety-order step scaling  
\* safety-order volume scaling  
\* maximum simultaneous trades  
\* multiple take-profit levels / partial exits  
\* trailing take profit  
\* stop loss  
\* trailing stop loss  
\* stop-loss timeout

Everything in the League is currently Spot, long-only and Paper/simulated trading. No real funds are used.

A public bot can be published in two ways: Performance only — everyone can follow the results, but the strategy settings remain private. or Public + Copyable — anyone can copy the exact configuration into their own Paper account and run an independent version.

I also wanted to avoid another problem with public strategy results: quietly changing the strategy after it starts performing badly. So public configurations are versioned. If the strategy settings materially change:

V1 closes → V2 starts.

The previous configuration and its performance period remain frozen instead of being silently rewritten. Copies also retain lineage, so over time you can see relationships like:

Original strategy → copy → modified variant

Each public experiment currently shows things like:

return · APY · max drawdown · win rate · age · closed trades · BTC benchmark · ETH benchmark

BTC and ETH are compared over the same period as the current bot version, rather than using some unrelated calendar period.

I built this inside LabNarrative, which I’m developing. The League is free to browse and the bots can be tested in Paper without putting real money at risk.

What I’m trying to figure out now is what would make the public record genuinely useful to people who already build or run trading bots.

What would you personally want to see before taking one of these results seriously?

Sharpe / Sortino?

Profit factor?

Average trade duration?

Exposure time?

Fees / slippage assumptions? (currently set on 0.2% for fees and 0.05 slippage for all)

Minimum number of closed trades?

Minimum time running before a bot should be considered mature?

Walk-forward or Monte Carlo information?

Something else?

Here’s the working League if you want to inspect what I mean:

\[https://app.labnarrative.com/league\](https://app.labnarrative.com/league)

Would especially like feedback from people who already build, test or run trading bots.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the thing i'd trust is the graveyard. show every version that got retired and when, and make any settings change stamp a new version instead of editing the old one in place.

clones cut the other way though. fifty variants of one idea and the best of them will look brilliant from selection alone, so ranking the survivors needs some penalty for how many siblings they had.

replies.author: GreatBreadfruit8139
replies.body:
Yep, the “graveyard” point is exactly how I’ve been thinking about it. I already made strategy changes create a new frozen version instead of rewriting the old one, so V1 stays there when V2 starts. I think the next useful step is making that history even more visible, including retired/failed versions rather than only the current survivor.

On the clone point though, I see it a bit differently. If 50 variants exist and one of them ends up being the survivor, I don’t think that automatically makes the survivor less valuable. What matters to me is what happens after it emerges.

If that bot keeps running unchanged, survives real market drawdowns, keeps its risk under control, and still performs after 50, 100, 200+ trades, then the market is continuously re-validating it.

So I’d rather show the context — how many variants existed, when this one was selected, how long it has kept running since, what drawdowns it survived — than permanently penalize it just because it came from a large family. to me.. t is not important how a strategy was discovered; what matters is whether it keeps surviving after discovery.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: frozen versions was the hard bit, so you're most of the way there. a retired tab sitting right next to the leaderboard would finish it. most leagues quietly drop the dead ones and that's exactly why nobody trusts them.

replies.author: GreatBreadfruit8139
replies.body:
Definitely, I like that. Since the versions are already frozen, a visible "Retired" tab feels like the natural next step.

I don’t want failed bots or old versions to disappear just because they’re no longer running. Keeping them beside the active leaderboard would make the history much more honest and also give context to the survivors.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, the survivors only mean something when you can see the ones that died next to them.

replies.author: TopPromise9775
replies.body:
I agree that the discovery path should not permanently disqualify the survivor, but it should determine where the evidence clock starts.



If one bot is selected from 50 after seeing their results, everything before that selection is discovery data. Freeze the selected configuration at that point and treat the selection timestamp as day zero. Only trades generated afterwards should count as confirmation of the survivor.



I'd show the family size, selection date, post-selection trade count, and whether another sibling can later replace it. Then the bot does not need a permanent penalty for having 49 siblings—but the audition period cannot also be counted as proof.

replies.author: GreatBreadfruit8139
replies.body:
Yeah, I think that’s a fair distinction.

I still don’t think the discovery path should permanently count against the survivor, but I agree that the confirmation clock should start when the configuration is frozen and selected.

So if one bot emerges from 50 variants, everything before selection is discovery. From that point on, the selected configuration has to prove itself independently. Then only the trades, drawdowns and market regimes it survives after that point count as confirmation.

I also like the idea of showing family size, selection date and post-selection trade count. That gives the full context without treating the bot as “invalid” just because it came from a large search space.

but I still care most about whether the survivor keeps performing after discovery and through real market drawdowns.

comments.author: dexoyo
comments.body: The problem is that bots look at the historical trend and try to make the trades based on that. They lack any real time metrics and usually fail to achieve the same levels in live execution

replies.author: GreatBreadfruit8139
replies.body:
Agreed.. that gap is exactly why I’m trying to keep this separate from backtesting.

These League bots are forward-running on current market data and only act on closed candles, so the performance record accumulates from that point onward rather than being fitted to historical candles.

But I still wouldn’t treat Paper performance as proof of Live performance. Real execution adds fills, slippage, latency, fees, exchange behavior, partial fills, etc. The useful question for me is whether a strategy survives forward testing first, and then how much of that behavior carries over once it runs Live.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Re "I built a public paper-trading League for crypto bots: What would make you trust the results?":

"The versioning-with-frozen-history piece already solves the biggest trust problem (silent strategy changes after a bad stretch), that alone puts this ahead of most public bot leaderboards. On your metric list, I'd prioritize in this order: minimum closed trades (I wouldn't trust anything under \~30-50, your earlier point about 6 trades in 4 days looking amazing is exactly why), profit factor over raw Sharpe since Sharpe gets distorted by DCA-style strategies with lumpy, non-normal return distributions, and exposure time, since a strategy that's only in the market 10% of the time and beats BTC needs a very different read than one that's fully exposed the whole period. Max drawdown relative to exposure time matters more than drawdown alone too, a -15% drawdown while 90% exposed is a different risk profile than -15% while barely in the market. Walk-forward/Monte Carlo info would be the most valuable addition for anyone trying to judge robustness rather than just performance, but I'd treat that as a 'nice to have' tier above the basics, since most public bot builders won't have that infra day one and the versioning/lineage system you've already built solves the more urgent trust problem (quiet rewrites) that walk-forward data doesn't address at all. Fee/slippage assumptions being fixed and disclosed (0.2%/0.05%) is good, though real slippage on thinner USDT pairs during volatility spikes can exceed that, worth flagging which pairs are more likely to see real-world slippage diverge from the assumption.

Good problem to be tackling, this kind of result-integrity work is something I think about a lot too with EventTrader's event-driven side." [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

replies.author: GreatBreadfruit8139
replies.body:
This is really useful, thanks. I agree that the basics should come before anything fancy.

I’m leaning toward making closed-trade count + exposure time much more prominent next, because both change how you interpret almost every other metric. A bot with 40 trades and 90% market exposure is a very different experiment from one with 40 trades and 10% exposure, even if the return and drawdown look similar.

Profit factor also makes sense to me for the League, especially for DCA-style systems where Sharpe can be a bit misleading. And I like your point about relating drawdown to exposure rather than treating drawdown as a standalone number.

Walk-forward / Monte Carlo is probably something I’d add later, after the public record itself is solid enough. Right now I care most about making sure people can’t rewrite history, hide failed versions, or make a tiny sample look mature..

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Glad that lines up. Surfacing closed-trade count and exposure time together as the primary framing (rather than burying them below return/drawdown) is the right instinct, most people scanning a leaderboard anchor on the headline return number first and only dig into sample size if something looks suspicious, so putting exposure and trade count front and center forces the right read before someone even gets to the performance numbers. Sequencing walk-forward/Monte Carlo for later makes sense too, integrity of the public record (no silent rewrites, no vanishing failed versions) is the foundation everything else sits on, robustness testing on top of a record people can't trust yet wouldn't actually move the needle. One thing worth considering as you build out the exposure-time display: showing it as a distribution over the bot's lifetime rather than a single average could help too, a bot that was 90% exposed for its first 10 trades and 10% exposed for the last 30 tells a different story than one with a flat 50% average the whole way through, and that kind of drift is exactly the sort of thing your versioning system would otherwise mask if it's not surfaced separately from the version-level rollup.
